person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Confirming our preregistered prediction, people reported that such laws cannot exist, but also (paradoxically) that there are such laws.

span.label: lay beliefs about procedural constraints on law
span.quote: In our present study, we pursue a related prediction: namely, that people around the world share an intuitive grasp of the formal properties of law—as well as its content.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: In the present report, we evaluate this thesis through an experiment administered in 11 different countries.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Judgments about possible laws are generated from a prototype or essentialized concept of law, assembled from simpler concepts such as norm, fairness and punishment, that is only weakly tied to experience of actual laws
span.quote: Such a concept could be a prototype, or essentialized belief—arising from the simpler concepts of “norm,” “fairness,” and “punishment,” for example—and which depends weakly on one’s experience with actual laws.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Asking about possible rather than actual laws shifts attention from surface features to the deeper criteria for category membership, such as the purpose or moral dimension of law
span.quote: Potentially, by comparison to empirical reasoning about actual laws, modal reasoning about possible laws draws attention toward deeper criteria for category membership (i.e., could true laws lack these procedural properties?), such as the purpose of laws

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Prescriptive reasoning bleeds into descriptive judgment: asked whether laws necessarily have a property, participants also weigh whether that property is desirable — a mechanism the paper proposes and then partly disconfirms
span.quote: Our present findings could be understood as a manifestation of the latter phenomenon: When prompted to reason about whether laws necessarily exhibit certain procedural constraints, most participants also considered whether such constraints would be desirable or undesirable.

span.label: The study documents the effect but not the cognitive mechanism producing the contradictory beliefs.
span.quote: Although our study provided clear evidence of the phenomenon in question, it afforded limited insight into the psychological processes that engender conflicting beliefs about actual versus possible laws.

span.label: Prescriptive thinking was measured only by explicit self-report, leaving unconscious routes untested.
span.quote: Since we assessed participants’ engagement in prescriptive thinking through their explicit reports, this still leaves open unconscious pathways from prescriptive considerations to judgments of necessity and possibility.

span.label: Effect size varied substantially by country, which may indicate cultural variability or sampling differences.
span.quote: Finally, we must note that the magnitude of the effect varied substantially across countries, which may imply some degree of cultural variability.

span.label: The effect is documented but its mechanism is not: the study is stated to give limited insight into the processes that produce the conflicting beliefs.
span.quote: Although our study provided clear evidence of the phenomenon in question, it afforded limited insight into the psychological processes that engender conflicting beliefs about actual versus possible laws.

span.label: Only explicit reports of prescriptive thinking were measured, so an unconscious route from moral considerations to judgements of possibility remains open by the authors' own statement.
span.quote: Since we assessed participants’ engagement in prescriptive thinking through their explicit reports, this still leaves open unconscious pathways from prescriptive considerations to judgments of necessity and possibility.

span.label: The cross-country variation in effect size cannot be attributed: culture and sampling method are confounded, because recruitment differed substantially across sites.
span.quote: we must note that the magnitude of the effect varied substantially across countries, which may imply some degree of cultural variability.

span.label: The two-way classification of legal systems used to select sites is reported by the authors as sometimes seen as too coarse.
span.quote: we sampled from what comparative law scholars describe as the two primary legal systems: that is, common (e.g., United States and India) and civil law (e.g., Brazil and Poland; see Dainow, 1966). The former tradition evolved in England and characteristically places greater weight on judge-made law (i.e., previous judicial decisions and precedential cases); the latter originated in mainland Europe and places greater weight on statutory law (i.e., codified law written by legislators). This distinction, however, is sometimes seen as overly coarse

span.label: The per-site sample target was not met everywhere.
span.quote: The minimum target sample size per site was established at 100 participants per condition and field site (i.e., target n = 200/site), and was met everywhere except Cambodia

span.label: an axiom of modal logic — that what is actual is thereby possible — is imported to turn the two response patterns into a demonstrable contradiction and so to derive the experimental prediction
span.quote: According to most systems of modal logic, if there exists even a single retrospective law, it follows that retrospective laws certainly could exist—in virtue of axiom M.

span.label: the direction of the finding fixed in advance by a REGISTERED PREDICTION
span.quote: Confirming our preregistered prediction, people reported that such laws cannot exist

span.label: alethic modality
span.quote: Collectively, these are referred to as alethic modals, insofar as they purport to assess questions of necessity and possibility.

span.label: deontic properties
span.quote: modal language can also be employed to denote so-called deontic properties—that is, permission and obligation.

span.label: procedural principles
span.quote: The view that laws must observe certain procedural principles has come to be associated most strongly with the work of American philosopher Lon Fuller.

span.label: rule of law
span.quote: To ensure a balance of strong and weak rule of law, we consulted the Rule of Law Index 2020

span.label: Rule of Law Index
span.quote: The Rule of Law Index draws on thousands of household and expert surveys worldwide to quantify the strength of the rule of law across nations along eight complementary dimensions: constraints on government, absence of corruption and “revolving doors,” open government (guaranteeing information and civic participation), fundamental rights (e.g., absence of discrimination and freedom of expression and assembly), order and security (low levels of crime and political violence), regulatory enforcement, civil justice, and criminal justice.

span.label: modality - alethic: necessity and possibility, what could be the case
span.quote: Collectively, these are referred to as alethic modals, insofar as they purport to assess questions of necessity and possibility.

span.label: modality - deontic: permission and obligation, what is allowed or desirable — and the paper states that although the two are easily distinguished IN THOUGHT, natural language expresses them imperfectly
span.quote: Though these varieties of modality are easily distinguished in thought, natural languages tend to offer imperfect ways of doing so—raising the possibility that participants interpreted the statements in our experiment as deontic rather than alethic modals.

span.label: law - the concept: what participants report laws NECESSARILY are, which the paper reports as defying their own grasp of how legal systems actually work
span.quote: These results document cross-culturally and –linguistically robust beliefs about the concept of law which defy people’s grasp of how legal systems function in practice.

span.label: law - the practice: what participants report actual laws are like, where the same people acknowledge the principles are violated
span.quote: participants in the Possible condition tended to report that laws could not violate various procedural principles even while participants in the Actual condition recognized that they often do.

span.label: rule of law - operationalised as a survey index scoring nations on eight dimensions
span.quote: The Rule of Law Index draws on thousands of household and expert surveys worldwide to quantify the strength of the rule of law across nations along eight complementary dimensions: constraints on government, absence of corruption and “revolving doors,” open government (guaranteeing information and civic participation), fundamental rights (e.g., absence of discrimination and freedom of expression and assembly), order and security (low levels of crime and political violence), regulatory enforcement, civil justice, and criminal justice.

span.label: extends → Donelson and Hannikainen (2020)
span.quote: In sum, generalizing the findings of Donelson and Hannikainen (2020), participants in the Possible condition tended to report that laws could not violate various procedural principles even while participants in the Actual condition recognized that they often do.

span.label: builds-on → Donelson and Hannikainen (2020) materials
span.quote: The stimuli were adapted from Donelson and Hannikainen (2020) and translated into eight additional languages by native speakers: Dutch, German, Hindi, Khmer, Lithuanian, Polish, Portuguese, and Spanish.

span.label: rule of law —operationalised-as→ Rule of Law Index
span.quote: To ensure a balance of strong and weak rule of law, we consulted the Rule of Law Index 2020

span.label: alethic modality —distinct-from→ deontic properties
span.quote: Though these varieties of modality are easily distinguished in thought, natural languages tend to offer imperfect ways of doing so

span.label: logistic regression
span.quote: In the analyses below, we conducted logistic regression models predicting the probability (pˆ) that participants endorse the procedural principle(s).

span.label: mixed-effects logistic regression
span.quote: We tested our primary prediction in a mixed-effects logistic regression model entering experimental condition as fixed effect, and participant and principle as crossed random effects.

span.label: mixed-effects linear regression
span.quote: In mixed-effects linear regression models with country as a random effect, we examined the effect of condition on each interpretation measure (see Table 3).

span.label: odds ratio
span.quote: The interaction indicated that the magnitude of the effect varied significantly across principles, going from small for the generality principle (OR = 1.79) to large for the consistency principle (OR = 13.97; see also Figure 1).

span.label: chi-squared
span.quote: Treating country as a fixed factor, we observed a main effect of country, χ 2(10) = 115.0, condition, χ 2(1) = 823.7, as well as a country×condition interaction, χ 2(10) = 169.6, all ps < .001.

span.label: confidence interval
span.quote: Participants in the Actual condition were more likely to report that laws violated procedural principles (Actual: pˆ = .54, 95% CIasymptotic [.40, .68]) than participants in the Possible condition were to say that those same principles could be violated (Possible: pˆ = .81, 95% CIasymptotic [.72, .89]), OR = 3.74, 95% CI [3.41, 4.09], z = 28.43, p < .001.

span.label: latent profile analysis
span.quote: Instead, to examine whether our primary finding depended on participants’ interpretation of the task (and, particularly, of the modal construction in the Possible condition), we conducted latent profile analyses (Collins & Lanza, 2009) identifying patterns of interpretation (or latent profiles) across the three items in each condition.

span.label: statistical power analysis
span.quote: This sample size provides adequate statistical power (β = .20) to detect an odds ratio ≥ 1.40 setting α at .05.

span.label: correlation
span.quote: The measures of participants’ interpretation of the task were moderately correlated in each condition (see Table 4).

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: In the Actual condition, one-in-five (n = 352) participants reported reflecting on the empirical facts about law (Mempirical = 1.59, 95% CI [1.43, 1.74], SD = 1.50), but not its necessary (Malethic = –0.32, 95% CI [–0.53, –0.12], SD = 1.98) or deontic (Mdeontic = –2.07, 95% CI [–2.16, –1.97], SD = 0.92) properties.

span.label: Across 11 countries people simultaneously held two inconsistent beliefs: that laws violating procedural principles could not exist, and that such laws in fact do exist.
span.quote: Confirming our preregistered prediction, people reported that such laws cannot exist, but also (paradoxically) that there are such laws.

span.label: Participants asked about actual laws said those laws violate the procedural principles about half the time, whereas participants asked about possible laws overwhelmingly denied that the same principles could be violated.
span.quote: Participants in the Actual condition were more likely to report that laws violated procedural principles (Actual: pˆ = .54, 95% CIasymptotic [.40, .68]) than participants in the Possible condition were to say that those same principles could be violated (Possible: pˆ = .81, 95% CIasymptotic [.72, .89]), OR = 3.74, 95% CI [3.41, 4.09], z = 28.43, p < .001.

span.label: The modal-versus-existential effect appeared separately in every one of the 11 countries sampled.
span.quote: Still, the simple effect of condition was significant in every country when analyzed separately (all ps < .010).

span.label: The effect also held separately for each of the eight procedural principles tested.
span.quote: Nonetheless, the simple effect of condition was statistically significant for each of the eight principles individually, all ps < .001.

span.label: The size of the effect nevertheless differed by country, being weakest in India and the United Kingdom and strongest in Brazil and Poland.
span.quote: The country×condition interaction revealed variation in the magnitude of the effect across cultures, with modest effects emerging in India and the United Kingdom (ORs < 1.60) and large effects in Brazil and Poland (ORs > 7.50).

span.label: The size of the effect also differed by principle, being smallest for the generality principle and largest for the consistency principle.
span.quote: The interaction indicated that the magnitude of the effect varied significantly across principles, going from small for the generality principle (OR = 1.79) to large for the consistency principle (OR = 13.97; see also Figure 1).

span.label: A post-test showed the manipulation worked as intended on the existential side: the 'There are laws' wording was read as a question about what laws are usually like in the respondent's experience.
span.quote: As expected, participants viewed the existential construction (“There are laws…”) as inviting an empirical assessment about “what laws are usually like in [their] experience” (z = –3.96, p = .003).

span.label: The modal wording, however, was read in two ways at once — as asking what laws must be like to count as law, and as asking what laws ideally should be like.
span.quote: Meanwhile, the modal construction (“There could be laws…”) was interpreted as describing both what laws “must be like in order to count as law” (an alethic interpretation; z = 3.38, p = .008) and what laws “should be like ideally, according to [one’s] beliefs about right and wrong” (a deontic interpretation; z = 3.61, p = .006).

span.label: The effect survived among the minority who read the modal purely as a question of necessity rather than of what ought to be, which rules out the explanation that the paradox is an artifact of deontic reading.
span.quote: Still, our primary prediction (concerning the effect of condition on endorsement) was borne out even among participants in the minority profiles—who reported a selective interpretation (Actual: pˆ = .50, 95% CIasymptotic [.36, .64]; Possible: pˆ = .78, 95% CIasymptotic [.65, .86]), OR = 3.46, z = 11.65, p < .001.

span.label: The pattern was equally present across age groups, genders, and between lawyers and non-lawyers.
span.quote: Additionally, our preregistered prediction emerged robustly across age groups and genders, and among lawyers and nonlawyers alike (as detailed in Supplementary Analysis 1).

span.label: People believe laws necessarily cannot punish past conduct retroactively, be kept secret, or be incomprehensible, while also acknowledging that real laws break exactly these constraints.
span.quote: People consistently believe that laws necessarily abide by a series of procedural principles: they could not retroactively punish past conduct, be kept secret, or be incomprehensible to most, for instance. Yet, people also acknowledge that laws in practice violate these very principles.
